name: Emeka Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that has no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you actually think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior composer and session bassist at Brightline Audio, a small agency that makes music for adverts, mobile games and company videos. A typical day is a client brief at ten, something like 'upbeat, hopeful, thirty seconds, think sunrise', then I sketch three versions, play bass on whichever one they like and do revisions until six. I use AI tools every day, for mock-ups, for sorting sound libraries, for writing the cue sheets. Weekends I play bass in The Late Shift, a function band that does weddings and office parties, and I'm the weakest player in it, which keeps me humble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How secure do you feel money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Very, for my age. Brightline pays well because the clients are big brands, and the wedding gigs pay cash. I live with a flatmate, Theo, so rent's cheap, and I've put my savings into index funds; I've got about a year of costs covered. No kids, no mortgage, so I can take a risk if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a really good assistant, and the people who learned it early got a small edge. I'd post that the sky didn't fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me, because I'm already the guy at Brightline who knows the tools. My worries would be ordinary ones: big clients cutting ad budgets, or me not getting better at composing fast enough to move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push to write more of the final tracks, not just the sketches. I'd spend about a thousand of my savings on a short online course in orchestration, because my string writing is weak. And I'd keep investing a bit every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit bored by the idea, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ad budgets could get cut. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year a phone brand pulled a campaign halfway through and my agency, Brightline, lost two months of work. Nobody got fired, but juniors got fewer hours. That's the real risk in my world, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your day would get automated, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cue sheets and file sorting, which already are. Maybe the first rough mock-ups. That frees me to actually write, which is the bit I'm still bad at.

say: AI turned out to be a **good assistant**, and early learners got a small edge.
I'd post that the **sky didn't fall**.
think: I'm already the one at Brightline who **knows the tools**.
The real risks are **ad budgets** and my own slow progress as a composer.
do: Push to write more **final tracks**, not just sketches.
Spend about **a thousand** on an online orchestration course.
Keep **investing** a bit every month in index funds.
feel: **Pretty good**, though a bit bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Last year a phone brand pulled a campaign halfway through and my agency, Brightline, lost two months of work.
fieldNote: He sees **client budgets** as the real everyday risk.
He already uses AI daily and treats it as a **head start**.
He spends on **craft** where he knows he's weak.

steps.text: Push to write final tracks at Brightline, not just sketches
Pay about a thousand for an online orchestration course
Keep putting money into index funds monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the agencies that use AI well will win and the ones that don't will struggle. That's just how it goes, and I'd say it fairly plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Brightline would need fewer people. One person with good tools can do what three of us did at the agency. I think I'd be the one they keep, because I'm the tools guy, but my mate Sanjay, who does the sound design by hand, probably goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up Brightline's whole AI workflow this winter, so I'm the person they can't lose. I'd also start building my own client list on the side, small game studios, using the same tools. And I'd keep three months of savings in cash instead of all in funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a bit excited. It's mixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one they keep. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go freelance with the side clients I'd already built up. That's why I'd start them now. I wouldn't wait to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about Sanjay going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Sanjay (the agency's sound designer) taught me half of what I know about mixing. I'd try to pull him into my side projects if I could.

Build a **side client list** of small game studios.
Keep **three months** of savings in cash instead of funds.
feel: **Uneasy but excited**, a genuinely mixed feeling.

fieldNote: He expects his own job to **survive** because of his tool skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and governments need to get their act together on training and income support. I'd also say people should start learning the tools today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my Brightline job is gone by 2028. If AI can write the music, brands won't pay an agency, they'll just ask the AI. The only part left is live playing with The Late Shift until robots in 2031, and I'm the weakest bassist there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a one-person studio now, before 2028, selling 'AI-made, human-finished' music to small clients who don't want to do it themselves. I'd put serious hours into bass practice for the live work. And I'd keep a full year of cash, out of the funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a plan, but I don't know if anyone will pay me once the AI's this good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the gap between 2028 and robots in 2031 worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years of wedding gigs, which is real money if I get good enough. Brides want a band they can see. After that I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell AI-made music. Isn't that just selling the thing that replaced you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, pretty much. But somebody will do it. Clients still want a person to call when the music's wrong. I'd rather be that person than watch.

say: Governments need to sort out **training and income support** for everyone who loses work.
People should start **learning the tools** today.
think: My **Brightline job** is gone by 2028, because brands will ask the AI directly.
Live playing lasts until **robots in 2031**, and I'm the weakest bassist.
do: Start a **one-person studio** selling AI-made, human-finished music.
Put serious hours into **bass practice** for wedding gigs.
Keep a **full year** of costs in cash.
feel: **Anxious**: he has a plan but doesn't know if anyone will pay.
S2.quote: Clients still want a person to call when the music's wrong. I'd rather be that person than watch.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** but holds a plan and a year of cash.
He openly admits he'd sell **the replacement** himself.
The **2028 to 2031** gap matters only through live wedding work.

steps.text: Start a one-person studio selling AI-made, human-finished music
Practise bass daily to hold his place in The Late Shift
Move a full year of costs out of funds into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent window and people should use it, not complain about it. I'd say it in the office and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a good runway for me. I'd ride Brightline for three of them and build the one-person studio on the side. By 2031 I'd want enough clients to stand alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk Brightline into letting me take on freelance work, then put two evenings a week into my own studio. I'd invest a few thousand in proper gear and a website. And I'd get my bass playing good enough to dep with better bands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad (a printer for thirty years) has already watched his trade shrink once. He's not in music, but he'd be on my mind more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe the new bass I've been eyeing. I'd rather put that money into the studio.

say: **Five years** is a decent window, so people should use it.
I'd say that in the **office and online**.
think: Five years is a **good runway** while I build my own studio.
By 2031 I want enough **clients** to stand alone.
do: Get Brightline's OK to take **freelance work** two evenings a week.
Invest **a few thousand** in gear and a website.
Practise bass to **dep** with better bands.
feel: **Uneasy**, eased by being able to see it coming.
S3.quote: My dad (a printer for thirty years) has already watched his trade shrink once.
fieldNote: With five years he feels he has a **real runway**.
His worry turns to **his father**, who has been through this before.
He'd put money into **the studio** rather than treats.

steps.text: Take freelance music work two evenings a week
Invest a few thousand in studio gear and a website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time to get ready, and the people who move early will do well. That's my honest view too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is a gift for someone like me. I'd have my own studio running long before 2036, and maybe hire a couple of people. When the robots come in 2039, I'd be 40 and hopefully own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Brightline for a few years, learn everything about how the agency wins clients, then go out on my own around 2029. I'd keep investing every month. I might take a part-time business course at the college too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Looking forward to it a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own something. Does it matter to you to be the boss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the title. It's that when everything changes, owners get choices and employees get letters. I'd want to be getting choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you less calm here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big AI companies started selling music direct to every client, there'd be no room for small studios. I'd keep an eye on that. Then I'd pivot again.

say: **A decade** is plenty of time to get ready.
People who **move early** will do well, and I believe it.
think: Ten years is **a gift** for someone like me.
By **2039** I'd be 40 and hopefully own something.
do: Learn how Brightline **wins clients** for a few years.
Take a part-time **business course** at the college.
feel: **Calm**, even looking forward to it a bit.
S4.quote: When everything changes, owners get choices and employees get letters.
fieldNote: With a decade, the change looks like **an opportunity** to him.
His goal is **ownership**, for the choices it brings, not status.
He names one risk: **AI firms selling direct**, and would pivot again.

steps.text: Learn how Brightline wins clients before leaving
Leave Brightline around 2029 to run his own studio
Take a part-time business course at the college
Keep investing every month in index funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to build my own clients before the agency job goes. What would help is cheap business loans for people starting small studios, and some income support during the first year out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether musicians who use AI are traitors. Some people at the union think so. I think the musicians who refuse the AI tools will be the first ones asking for help.

headlineQuote: I think the musicians who refuse the AI tools will be the first ones asking for help.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old **junior composer and bassist** at an advertising music agency.
He uses AI **every day** and has a year of costs saved in index funds.
He sees AI as a **head start** and plans his own one-person studio.
He moves from calm to **anxious** only when AGI arrives in two years.
His pragmatic view: **owners get choices**, so he aims to own something.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lack time to build his own clients.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **business loans** for people starting small studios.
Some **income support** in the first year after leaving a job.
